skills.name: Primary storage: RAM and ROM; storage units

note.text:
Primary (main) storage is directly accessed by the CPU.
• RAM (random access memory): holds the programs and data in use; it can be read and written; it is volatile (contents lost when power goes off). More RAM lets more programs run smoothly.
• ROM (read-only memory): holds the start-up instructions (BIOS/firmware); it can only be read; it is non-volatile.
Units: 8 bits = 1 byte; 1 KB = 1024 bytes; 1 MB = 1024 KB; 1 GB = 1024 MB; 1 TB = 1024 GB.

sections.heading: Memory the CPU uses directly
sections.text:
Primary storage is memory the CPU can access directly. There are two kinds.
• RAM (random access memory) holds the programs and data you are using now: the document you are typing, the browser, the game. It can be read and written. It is volatile: when the power goes off, its contents are lost.
• ROM (read-only memory) holds instructions needed to start the computer (BIOS/firmware). It can only be read, and it is non-volatile.

sections.heading: Storage units
sections.text:
• {8} bits = {1} byte (enough for one character).
• {1} kilobyte (KB) = {1024} bytes.
• {1} megabyte (MB) = {1024} KB.
• {1} gigabyte (GB) = {1024} MB.
• {1} terabyte (TB) = {1024} GB.
Each unit is {1024} ({2} to the power {10}) times the one before, because computers count in binary.

sections.heading: How much RAM?
sections.text:
If RAM is full, the computer moves data to the much slower disk, and everything slows down. More RAM lets more programs run at once smoothly.
A phone might have {4} GB of RAM; a laptop {8} GB or more.
Always save your work: unsaved work in RAM is lost in a power cut.
